overview: This layer shows Malta and Gozo during part of British colonial rule, from 1878 to 1920. The islands were a Mediterranean imperial stronghold as well as homes, workplaces and farming communities. The map dates mark selected coverage: they are neither the beginning nor the end of British rule. This card concentrates on colonial daily life and the movement towards self-government.

periods.title: Colonial islands and demands for a voice
periods.summary: Schooling, transport and medicine changed while Maltese campaigners pressed for more control over their own affairs.

items.text: Many government schools around 1880 occupied rented houses. Rooms designed for families could become overcrowded classrooms with poor ventilation. Historian Conrad Thake describes the difficulty of adapting these buildings: adding pupils did not magically add fresh air or elbow room.

School toilets also drew fierce criticism. Keenan complained about offensive smells at schools including Cospicua and Senglea, and many schoolhouses lacked playgrounds. A child’s school day could therefore involve both cramped lessons and very little proper space for running about afterwards.

In his report published in 1880, Patrick Keenan said primary schools reached fewer than two-fifths of children aged five to ten. He also reported that most pupils of those ages were still learning letters or a primer. These are the inspector’s findings, showing how uneven access to schooling remained.

A surviving lace skirt from the late nineteenth or early twentieth century was made in separate pieces by several skilled workers. Differences in its stitches help reveal that teamwork. Its thirty-two panels were sewn together by hand: this was an elaborate project, not a garment that appeared at the push of a button.

The same skirt has evidence that someone was once sewn into it for an occasion. Getting undressed meant cutting the fastening threads. Lace-makers worked with bobbins on a pillow or roller, controlling threads with great care. The surviving luxury garment reveals both fashionable display and the labour behind it.

Malta’s railway began in 1883 and its tram system in 1905. The systems linked Valletta with places including Mdina and the Three Cities, carrying people and goods more quickly than traditional horse carriages. Steam whistles became part of island life before growing motor traffic helped displace the rail services.

Themistocles Zammit investigated goats during the search for the cause of Malta fever. His 1905 Royal Society paper reported experiments on their susceptibility to the infection. A familiar farm animal had become a scientific clue in understanding an illness that troubled the islands.

Research connected infected goats’ milk with the transmission of brucellosis, also called Malta fever. British military establishments replaced goats’ milk with tinned or condensed milk, greatly reducing their problem. Civilian acceptance was slower and disputed. Finding a cause and persuading a whole society to change its habits were different jobs.

In August 1914, the outbreak of the First World War prompted Malta’s first official local currency notes. There were five denominations in shillings and pounds. They were a temporary precaution and were withdrawn the following year, after which the islands again depended on currency imported from Britain.

After the war, bread and other essential foods were scarce and expensive. Dockyard dismissals, new taxes and unequal treatment of Maltese and British workers added to public anger. For many households, arguments about colonial government were closely connected with the practical question of affording dinner.

University students protested, newspapers faced censorship and activists demanded more political rights. These tensions contributed to the revolt of 7 June 1919, remembered as Sette Giugno. Heritage Malta’s exhibition places the event within wider demands for self-government after the First World War.

A new constitution in 1921, just after this map layer ends, gave the Maltese a greater role in running their country. It remained a step within colonial rule. Independence came in 1964, and Malta became a republic in 1974, after further political struggles and constitutional changes.

The newspaper of 25 April 1912 carries the title “IL HABIB”, meaning “The Friend”. This preserves its printed spelling rather than silently replacing it with modern “Il-Ħabib”. Its front page lists a postal subscription costing three shillings a year in Malta and Gozo. Written Maltese carried news, arguments and everyday information into readers’ homes.

ending.text: The 1920 endpoint is a map cutoff. Colonial government continued after the 1921 constitution. Malta gained independence in 1964 and became a republic in 1974; the people and islands continued through those changes.
